Impossible Metrics.short_definition: A performance bar kept out of reach through vague, shifting or contradictory criteria, so the shortfall is then credited to the person.
Impossible Metrics.core_meaning: A performance bar kept out of reach through vague, shifting or contradictory criteria, so the shortfall is then credited to the person.
Impossible Metrics.expanded_definition: These are targets that cannot be met as set: the criteria are vague, the number rises when you get close, two requirements pull against each other, or the resources do not match the demand. The shortfall is then read as a personal failing and not as a property of the target. Hard targets are normal. What marks the pattern is that nobody under similar conditions has met it, the finish line moves, and the record fills with misses. It is a standing bar, not a single doomed task.
Impossible Metrics.plain_language_summary: The bar you are measured against keeps moving or can't be met, so you always fall short, and the shortfall is put down to you.
Impossible Metrics.why_this_matters: Failure is built into the standard but credited to the person, so effort rises while the record fills with shortfalls. People in this position often work longer and doubt themselves more, and the paper trail starts to read like proof of a problem with them.
what_it_is: A target whose success criteria are vague enough, such as 'be more strategic' or 'show more ownership', to be reread after the fact.
A number that rises just as you approach it, or a new condition added when you meet the old one.
Contradictory demands, like cutting costs and doubling quality with the same team and hours.
Resources that do not match the load, such as one person asked to produce the output of three roles.
Found in jobs, schools, households ('a clean home') and caregiving. The harm lies in the growing record of misses.
what_it_sounds_like: Hit ninety-five percent and we'll talk. Then, at ninety-six: 'Now we need ninety-eight.'
It just needs to be more polished, with no description of what polished means.
I want it fast, perfect and cheap, and I'm not discussing which one gives.
You'll know it when you see it, offered as the specification.
Other people manage, with nobody named.
Last quarter's target was met, but that was the easy one.
what_it_is_not: High but achievable standards that others in the same role have met under the same conditions. Those are demanding, not impossible.
Stretch goals framed openly as aspirations rather than pass or fail.
A bar you have cleared before under similar conditions.
A target raised openly for a stated reason, such as a new contract, with resources raised to match.
A manager still working out what they want who clarifies when asked.
Hard performance management that is specific, with written criteria and support.
this_may_be_it_when: You cannot find anyone who has met this bar under the same conditions.
The goal changes shape just as you near it.
Asked what success looks like, you get adjectives instead of numbers or examples.
Time or resources you asked for to hit the number are refused while the number stays.
Your misses are recorded carefully, while what you did hit goes unrecorded.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Others in your role have hit the target and can describe how.
The criteria are written, stable, and applied to your peers.
When you hit it, it is recognised as a pass.
Asking for clarity gets a specific answer.
Resources were adjusted when you asked.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A manager can be unclear because the company is unclear. Vague goals often start with vague strategy.
Targets set at the start of the year from forecasts may later prove optimistic.
Real competitive pressure sometimes raises standards because customers expect more.
common_false_positives: A sales quota that is hard but hit by half the team.
A teacher grading to a rubric that is demanding but published in advance.
A new boss's higher standard announced with training and time to reach it.
discernment_questions: Has anyone met this standard under conditions like mine, and can I name them?
Can I write down what a pass looks like, and would the other person sign it?
Did the target move after I got near it?
Are the contradictions in the demand ever acknowledged, or only my shortfall?
Are my hits recorded as carefully as my misses?
less_concerning_if: Others reach the target and the criteria are in writing.
When you meet it, it is recognised without a new condition appearing.
You can point out a contradiction in the demand and have it adjusted.
more_concerning_if: The record of misses is being used for pay, hours, discipline or dismissal.
The same bar is not applied to others in the same role.
You are told that asking for clarity shows a bad attitude.
pattern_over_time_signs: You work longer hours each quarter for results that are no better received.
Review meetings are mostly lists of what is missing.
You write more and more things down, because the definitions keep changing.
You stop expecting to ever hear 'that's done'.
Impossible Metrics.repair_check: Repair would be a standard you could pass: criteria written down, numbers fixed for a stated period, and a result recorded as met when you meet it. An apology for the stress while the same target stays in place changes the tone, not the bar.
Impossible Metrics.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the definition of done in writing and see whether it comes back. A specific answer that stays put for the period you agree is respect for the request. If the definition arrives and then changes again, the written version has not become the standard.
Impossible Metrics.psychological_mechanism: When a standard cannot be reached, effort stops translating into success, and people tend to turn the blame inward because the standard is presented as reasonable. Never being able to finish can create a constant sense of falling behind. The growing record of misses can then be read, by others and by the person, as evidence of a personal trait.
Impossible Metrics.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe working harder for less sense of achievement, taking work home, and dreading review days. Some begin to believe they are bad at jobs they once did well. Others stop volunteering ideas, or reach burnout without ever having had one clear win to point to.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for clarity: 'What would a pass look like on this one? If I hit these numbers by the end of the month, would that count as met?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State the contradiction: 'Faster and more thorough both need more time or more people. Which one would you like me to put first?'
response_options.disengagement: Stop adding unpaid effort to chase a moving number. Work to the stated standard in normal hours and see whether the result is recorded.
response_options.support_seeking: Compare notes with peers in the same role: what are they measured on, and do they hit it? A mentor or trusted colleague outside your chain can give a view.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Ask for the criteria in an email and confirm after each conversation what was agreed. Keep a dated log of results. HR, a union or an ombuds can compare your targets with your peers'.

Impossible Metrics.boundary_script: "I want to meet this target. To do that I need to know exactly what counts as meeting it, in writing, and what resources I'll have. Could we agree that today and review against it in a month?"
Impossible Metrics.safety_note: This is rarely a physical danger. It becomes a livelihood issue when the record of misses feeds a dismissal, a demotion, or the end of a visa tied to the job. If a performance plan or warning appears, keep copies of the targets and your results, and speak to a union representative, employment lawyer or legal aid before signing anything.
misuse_warning: Calling every hard target impossible can excuse a standard you could actually meet. Test it against the people who did meet it.
Treating a manager's vague wording as proof of a plan against you ignores that vagueness is often just an unfinished idea. Ask for specifics first.
Impossible Metrics.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Setting Up to Fail is one assignment with conditions stacked against it; Impossible Metrics is a standing bar that follows you from task to task. Comparative Devaluation holds you up against other people; here the comparison is to a number, or to unnamed peers who 'manage', that nobody has met. Shame Installation turns a failure into a judgement of who you are, while impossible metrics supply the failures.

Setting Up to Fail.short_definition: Giving someone a task under conditions that make success unlikely, then treating the failure as proof of their inadequacy.
Setting Up to Fail.core_meaning: Giving someone a task under conditions that make success unlikely, then treating the failure as proof of their inadequacy.
Setting Up to Fail.expanded_definition: This is one assignment with the odds stacked: a deadline too short, a budget too small, information held back, or authority missing for what is being asked. When it fails, the conditions vanish from the retelling and only the outcome remains. Plenty of tasks are hard, and plenty of resources are scarce for everyone. The pattern shows when requests for what is needed are brushed aside and the failure is later cited as a fact about you.
Setting Up to Fail.plain_language_summary: You are handed a job few people could finish with what you were given, and when it goes wrong, the blame lands on you and not on the set-up.
Setting Up to Fail.why_this_matters: Conditions disappear from the account and only the outcome remains, so a predictable failure becomes durable evidence about the person who was handed it. One failed project can be quoted in reviews and decisions about you long after the conditions are forgotten.
what_it_is: A single task or project whose conditions make success unlikely: an impossible timeline, a thin budget, no access to people or data.
Often delivered with a vote of confidence ('I know you can do it'), which makes refusing awkward.
Paired with requests for more time, staff or information being declined, delayed or ignored.
Followed by a retelling that drops the conditions: 'the launch failed' instead of 'the launch had two weeks and no designer'.
Not limited to work. A household move, a school project or a group trip can be handed to one person the same way.
what_it_sounds_like: I know it's due Friday and the data isn't in yet, but I have faith in you.
There's no budget for that, just make it work.
You don't need to see the client brief. Just draft it.
Take the lead on the audit, but don't involve finance.
Why did you let it fail? I gave you everything you needed.
Remember the Henderson project? That's why I can't trust you with this.
I'd help, but I think you should learn to do it on your own.
what_it_is_not: Hard tasks with real constraints, which are ordinary work.
Resources that are unavailable to everyone, not withheld from you.
Something that turned out harder than anyone anticipated.
A stretch assignment given with the risk acknowledged openly and a fallback in place, so a miss is understood to be fine.
Clumsy delegation by someone who underestimated the task and revises the plan when told.
A pilot whose purpose is to test a plan, where its failing is the useful result.
this_may_be_it_when: Asked for what you need, you get a refusal without a reason.
Others on the team got more time or support on comparable tasks.
Information or authority you needed was missing, and it could easily have been shared.
The record afterwards leaves out the constraints you flagged beforehand.
The failure gets cited later in unrelated conversations.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You and the person assigning it both knew the odds and agreed to go ahead for a stated reason.
Your requests for support were met, even partly.
A post-mortem examined the conditions as well as your work.
Peers on similar tasks had the same conditions.
The missing information turned out to be unavailable to everybody.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Planners often underestimate how long things take, so the deadline may reflect a poor estimate.
Budgets get cut mid-quarter, and the person who assigned the task may have no say.
A busy person delegates with a thin brief because they don't have time to write a fuller one.
common_false_positives: A start-up where everyone is stretched and the founder's own tasks are just as tight.
A coach's tough preparation set where the difficulty is the point and the athlete knows it.
A project that failed because the market changed under everyone involved.
discernment_questions: Could a competent person with these resources and this time have succeeded, and can I name someone who did?
Did I flag the constraints in writing before I began?
How were my requests for help handled, and how were other people's?
When it failed, was the set-up discussed at all, or only me?
Is this failure being brought up in later, unrelated situations?
less_concerning_if: The shortfall in resources is shared by comparable tasks and acknowledged openly.
Requests for help get a real answer, even if the answer is no.
The review looks at the conditions as well as the outcome.
more_concerning_if: The same person hands you doomed tasks repeatedly while others get workable ones.
Your written flags of risk are ignored and the failure is then recorded as yours alone.
Past failures are cited to justify removing responsibility, pay or a role.
pattern_over_time_signs: You begin sending a note in writing before each task listing what you would need.
The assignments you are offered shrink after each failure, or only the doomed ones arrive.
You catch yourself volunteering for fewer things.
Colleagues or family members remember the failure but not its conditions.
Setting Up to Fail.repair_check: Repair starts with the retelling. A person who has noticed this goes back to the people who heard that you failed the launch, corrects the account to include the deadline and missing staff, and gives the next assignment the resources it needs. Praise for effort that leaves the record unchanged is a different thing.
Setting Up to Fail.boundary_respect_check: Watch the next request you send. If you ask in writing for what the task needs and get a yes, a partial yes with a reason, or a clear no that is noted in the plan, you were taken seriously. A cheerful 'you'll manage' and no reply is a different answer.
Setting Up to Fail.psychological_mechanism: Failure tends to be read as information about the person, and the conditions that produced it fade from memory faster than the outcome. If whoever set the task also describes the result, that account can become the accepted one. People who fail under such conditions often blame their own skill, since the constraints felt like background and the result felt personal.
Setting Up to Fail.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe replaying the project to find what they should have done, losing confidence in tasks they once handled well, and dreading the next hand-off. Some start to avoid anything visible. Others say that once they wrote down the original conditions they felt a grim relief, because the failure looked different on paper.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about the gap before starting: 'This needs three people and I have one, with two weeks. What would you like me to drop?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Put your concerns on record: 'I'll start, but I want it noted that without the client data this deadline is not realistic.'
response_options.disengagement: Decline the version of the task that cannot be done and offer the version that can. Do not absorb the shortfall quietly with overtime.
response_options.support_seeking: Walk a mentor or friend outside the project through the brief, deadline and resources, and ask whether they would have seen it as doable.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Send a short written summary after the assignment conversation: scope, deadline, resources, what you asked for. Keep it for any review, and use HR or a union representative if failures are cited in your evaluation.

Setting Up to Fail.boundary_script: "I want this to go well, so I'm saying now that I can't finish it by Friday without the sales figures. If I can have them by Tuesday, I can meet the deadline."
Setting Up to Fail.safety_note: On its own this is not a physical danger. It becomes a livelihood matter when failed assignments are used in firing, probation or job decisions that affect an immigration status. Keep the written brief, your flags and the outcome together, and ask a union representative, employment lawyer or legal aid service for advice before attending a disciplinary meeting alone.
misuse_warning: Calling a hard assignment a set-up can stop you learning from a failure that was partly yours. Ask whether the conditions were the same for others.
Using the label on a manager whose estimate was simply wrong turns a fixable planning problem into a feud. Start with the written flag.
Setting Up to Fail.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Impossible Metrics is a standing bar that stays out of reach across all your work; Setting Up to Fail is one assignment loaded against you. Scapegoating blames you for a failure that belonged to the group, whereas here the task was handed to you alone and the blame is for that one assignment. Intimidation threatens consequences; here nothing is threatened, and the record carries the consequence.
